title: ATM service and dispense strategy
idea: The core design is one ATM facade that runs authenticate and withdraw, and reaches the bank and the note planner only through injected interfaces.

analogy.text: A cashier at a bank counter. The cashier follows one routine, but phones head office to approve and follows a rule card to pick notes.
analogy.breaks: A cashier can bend the rule card; a Java strategy cannot.

points: `ATM` is a facade: the screen calls `insertCard`, `enterPin` and `withdraw`.
`BankService` hides the network call to the bank, so tests use memory.
`DispensePlanner` is the strategy pattern: each note-picking rule is a class.
Plan notes first, debit second, dispense last; a failed plan moves no money.

steps.caption: The customer, already authenticated, asks for Rs 2,600.
The `ATM` facade checks the session and starts the withdrawal.
The planner picks notes from stock: one 2000, one 500, one 100. No money has moved yet.
Only now does the bank debit the account and return a transaction id.
The dispenser lowers its note counts and pushes the notes out.
The screen shows TX-1 and the notes. The facade hid every step.
Next the customer asks for Rs 9,000. The notes left cannot make it, so the ATM refuses before calling the bank.

code.title: Facade and interfaces
code.caption: The core flow. Bank and planner are interfaces passed in. The demo PIN check is a stand-in; page 7 checks a salted hash.

walk.text: Wire the ATM with an in-memory bank, a greedy planner and loaded notes.
Wrong PIN, right PIN, then three withdrawals and the final state.
Two interfaces: the bank and the note planner. Each is a swap point.
Greedy takes as many large notes as fit, then moves to smaller ones.
`withdraw` plans first, debits second, dispenses last. A bank refusal dispenses nothing.
The bank's `debit` is `synchronized` and refuses to overdraw. Page 5 explains why.

code.title: A new strategy
code.caption: Greedy can miss an amount that the notes can make. A backtracking planner is added as a new class; ATM is not edited.

walk.text: Stock: one 500 note and three 200 notes. Ask both planners for Rs 600.
Each planner gets the same stock; print its plan or a refusal.
A new class implements the same interface, so nothing else changes.
Try the most of each note first, then fewer, until the rest fits exactly.

pitfalls: Do not debit before checking the notes can make the amount; it forces a reversal.
Do not add `if (greedy)` branches inside ATM; add a new planner class.
Keep the bank behind an interface; tests must not need a real network.

quiz.q: What does ExactChange print for GreedyPlanner?
quiz.why: Greedy takes the 500 first. Rs 100 is left, and no 100 notes exist, so it refuses. Three 200s would have worked.

takeaway: One facade for the screen; every changing rule behind an injected interface.

starters: Is backtracking fast enough with four note types?
Should the planner also prefer to keep large notes in stock?
How would I test the ATM without a bank connection?
